subject: advert for the spOccupancy R package

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: advert for the spOccupancy R package
parts:
Dear all

over the holidays I've been exploring the new spOccupancy R package, which lets you fit spatial and non-spatial occupancy models to large and very large data sets (see https://www.jeffdoser.com/files/spoccupancy-web/). And I must say that it's really cool ! For map-making in the SDM business, accommodating spatial autocorrelation, i.e., fitting spatial models, can be a real plus. Now this can be done in JAGS, Nimble etc, but is much harder for the not-so-initiated. And: run times for spatial models can be huge and convergence rates terrible.

spOccupancy (along with only a very small handful other R packages, including stocc, hSDM and also the brand-new ubms) makes spatial occupancy modeling fairly easy even for beginners and lets you fit several types of occupancy models to even very large data sets overnight.

Here are some species distribution maps for the Rock bunting in Switzerland. I had detection/nondetection data from about 25k 1km2 quadrats (for a total modeled domain of 42k such quadrats). Original temporal resolution was 140 daily occasions, but R choked on that on my laptop, so I aggregated to weekly occasions. In occupancy I added 17 environmental predictors in both linear and squared form, and I had survey date in linear and squared form in detection. I fit a non-spatial model and then a spatial model with exponential spatial correlation and considering only 15 nearest-neighbours at each site (a significant comp/stats "trick" explained in more detail in the spOccupancy documentation). The non-spatial model ran in 5 hours, while the spatial model ran in 11. Convergence was good for the former and so-so for the latter (biggest Rhat was about 1.3, so if this were for a publication I would have run much longer). WAIC said that the spatial model was far better than the non-spatial model.

The maps on the left show predicted occupancy probability (posterior means) and its uncertainty (posterior standard deviations) from the non-spatial model. Comparing this map with the density map in the latest Swiss breeding bird atlas (Knaus et al. 2018), this SDM overpredicts a lot, showing moderate probabilities in a far too big region, while not showing the density centres well enough. In contrast, the spatial model (on the right) gets rid of a lot of the "unnecessary yellow" in the occupancy map and shows the real centres of the Swiss Rock bunting distribution in much sharper detail (albeit with more uncertainty). The reason for why the spatial model predicts so much better is the presence in the model of a spatial random field in occupancy, which is shown at the bottom right. You can think of this as a sort of spatially smeared out occupancy residual map, which corrects for differences between the observed data and what is predicted by the covariates alone.

Fitting this model in JAGS with splines to accommodate spatial autocorrelation might perhaps haven taken 2 weeks, so spOccupancy is a real asset if you want to fit spatial occupancy models especially to large data sets.

So I wish you good luck with your own spatial occupancy modeling !

Best regards  --- Marc
